children: An AI credit event or a collapse in global oil prices? Just two potential surprises, BofA suggests
From AI to the Fed, Bank of America identifies what surprises may lie in store for investors next year.

What might surprise investors in 2027? To the upside: massive China fiscal stimulus, a collapse in the oil price and a political compromise in which Democrats backstop artificial intelligence in exchange for universal healthcare. To the downside: an AI credit event leading to a plunge in chip pricing and markets suddenly discovering - to their intense discomfort -that the Federal Reserve really means business with its 2% inflation target.

These are the unexpected bull and bear developments, outlined by Bank of America, that might ambush investors in 2027. They were included in the investment bank's year-ahead outlook published Monday, and lead-authored by chief investment strategist Michael Hartnett. However, while these are the about-turns that might wrongfoot investors heading into next year, they don't represent his base-case scenario.

For Hartnett, 2027 is going to require a tactical gameplan. The bank's economists expect the global rate-hiking cycle to peter out sometime in the spring, as inflation rolls over, and the second half of the year to be altogether more positive as an easing narrative in monetary policy takes over. Putting numbers on these forecasts, Hartnett anticipates another 38 central bank hikes between now and June, and then 21 cuts in the second half.

This soft-landing scenario is where Hartnett gets tactical. Upside for risk assets might start to develop as the hiking cycle fades and if Bank of America's below-consensus global earnings growth estimates of around 10% prove accurate, then stocks worldwide should increase between 4% and 8%. Price-to-earnings multiples for major indices are no longer intimidating with the MSCI All Cap World Index ACWI trading on roughly 14 times, and excluding the U.S, just 11 times, well below its 10-year average.

If, and when, these easier financial conditions develop around March to April, and having kept some gunpowder dry, Hartnett and his colleagues recommend investors look towards cyclicals for performance with his handful of Cs most favored: chips SOX, commodities COMB, crypto (BTCUSD) and consumer stocks VCR.
Bank of America expects a soft landing but still thinks consensus EPS forecasts are too high, so showing tactical patience recommended.

The grand secular themes of the 2020s so far have been encapsulated in the acronyms that Hartnett always likes to conjure up:  ABB, for anything but bonds, ABC, for anything but China CN:SHCOMP, ABD, for anything but the dollar DXY,  and AI, which to him means all-in on artifical intelligence. Of these, he thinks ABB is now exhausted and predicts positive returns for bonds and ABC looks risky if the Chinese government embarks on major fiscal stimulus to revitalize its moribund economy.
ABD and AI may be on pause for now, Hartnett notes, but could well return to fashion in the second half of 2027.

There are, Hartnett points out, eminently realistic bubble and bust scenarios possible next year. If the AI boom can be sustained then a S&P 500 SPX target of 8,888 is within reach. That will require Democrats and Republicans reaching some form of political compromise on healthcare and data centers.
$1.3tn AI capex expected in '27 despite -$283bn FCF. Any downgrading in projected capex leaves the market vulnerable

If there's a hard landing for the U.S. economy, something only 3% of fund managers polled in November predicted, then 5% to 6% forecasts for gross domestic product, and 15% to 20% earnings per share growth, are way too optimistic. In that instance, the S&P 500 sliding to 6,666 is possible and inevitably, Hartnett has an acronym to deal with it: GRAB.
This would involve a higher allocation to government bonds, real estate VNQ , AAA defensive assets and bullion (GC00).
